I like building across the stack, from low-level systems work to web apps and applied AI. I enjoy turning messy problems into working, well-structured prototypes.
summary:
Earth Jukebox is a web jukebox for NASA Earth Information Center visualizations. Pick one and listen. Nothing is pre-recorded: the browser makes the sound live from the visualization’s own frames.

About twenty times a second, the app shrinks the current frame to a 64 by 32 grid, checks each cell’s brightness, colour and change, and a small rulebook per track turns that into notes. Lightning flashes become plucked notes, pitched by their height in the picture and placed left or right to match. Sea surface temperature becomes a slow six-voice chord: warm water sounds low and full, cold water high and thin, and moving currents add a shimmer. Night lights become a pulse that speeds up as the map brightens, with falling tones where light was lost and rising tones where it was gained.

Each track has an audio legend whose buttons play one sound and say what it means, a line of text describing what you’re hearing, and full keyboard control. Blind and low-vision visitors can follow how the planet is changing, and sighted visitors can hear what they’re seeing. No AI model writes the music. The same frame always gives the same sound.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Earth Jukebox is a website that turns NASA visualizations into sound. It has five clips taken from three Earth Information Center visualizations: lightning seen from the International Space Station (split into three parts), sea surface currents and temperature, and the change in night lights. You pick a clip, learn what each sound means from the audio legend, and press Play. The picture and its soundscape run together, so if you pause the picture, the sound stops too. You can also pick out one part of the picture and listen to just that part, either with buttons or with a square that follows your mouse.

HOW IT WORKS
About 20 times a second, the current video frame is drawn onto a hidden canvas that’s 64 cells wide and 32 tall. Overlays like dates and colour bars get blanked out first. Then each cell gets four numbers: brightness, hue, saturation, and how much it changed since the last frame. Each track turns those numbers into sound in its own way.

Lightning: when a cell suddenly gets more yellow, it plays one plucked note. Flashes higher up in the picture sound higher. Flashes on the left come out of your left ear and flashes on the right come out of your right. Bigger flashes are louder. I listen for yellow rather than brightness because the white orbit line, the clouds and the stars are bright too, and I didn’t want them making noise.

Ocean: the map is cut into six regions, and each one has a single sustained voice. To work out the water temperature, the app checks each colour against the picture’s own colour bar. Warm water sounds low and full, and cold water sounds high and thin. West plays in your left ear and east in your right, and moving currents add a shimmer on top. The clip covers a full year, so you can hear the northern voices drop and rise with the seasons while the southern ones go the other way.

Night lights: the brighter the picture is overall, the more notes play each second. A note’s pitch comes from its latitude, and its left or right position comes from its longitude. On the change map, orange areas (where light was lost) play falling tones and purple areas (where light was gained) play rising ones. Zoomed-in views get a short rising phrase.

To keep it easy on the ears, every pitch comes from the same pentatonic scale. Values are smoothed between frames, new notes are capped at roughly 12 a second, and everything goes through one shared reverb and a limiter.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
The main goal is that someone who can’t see the screen can still use these visualizations. The audio legend teaches each sound before you hear it in context, and a line of text describes what’s playing right now. Every control has a proper name and works from the keyboard, and changes are announced through a single polite live region. Sighted visitors get something out of it too: the seasonal swing in the ocean track is honestly easier to hear than to spot by eye. Since the rules only look at the rendered frames, the same idea could work for other visualizations. You’d just write a small rulebook for each one.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES
It’s built with TypeScript, React and Vite. The sound comes from Tone.js on top of the Web Audio API, and the frames are read with the Canvas 2D API. It’s hosted on GitHub Pages and deployed with GitHub Actions. I used FFmpeg once to cut and re-encode the clips. There’s no backend and no machine-learning model anywhere in it.

CREATIVITY
Nobody composed this music, and no AI generated it. Fixed rules work it out from the picture, in your browser, as you watch. The legend buttons use the exact same rules as the live track, so the legend can’t fall out of sync with what you actually hear.
